questions.question: You start the 8-puzzle with an odd number of inverted pairs. Which target grid can you rule out without any searching?
options: Any grid with an even number of inverted pairs
Any grid with the blank in a corner
Any grid with an odd number of inverted pairs
Any grid where tile 1 is not in the top-left
questions.explanation: Inversion parity is preserved by every move and starts odd, so it is invariant. A grid with even parity makes the predicate false, so it is unreachable.

questions.question: What is the difference between a preserved predicate and an invariant?
options: They are two names for the same thing
Preserved is about single transitions; invariant is about all reachable states
Invariant is about single transitions; preserved is about all reachable states
Preserved predicates only apply to finite machines
questions.explanation: Preserved means each move keeps P true. Invariant means P holds in every reachable state. Preserved plus true at the start gives invariant, by the Invariant Principle.

questions.question: Swap sort repeatedly swaps any adjacent out-of-order pair. Why must it stop?
options: Because the list gets shorter after each swap
Because it always swaps the leftmost bad pair first
Because the number of inverted pairs is a natural number that drops by exactly 1 each swap
Because the largest element moves right every time
questions.explanation: The inversion count is a derived variable in the natural numbers that strictly decreases, so there can be at most as many swaps as the starting inversion count. The choice of pair does not matter.

questions.question: A machine has a derived variable that strictly decreases on every transition, but the machine runs forever. What must be true?
options: The derived variable is always a natural number
The machine has no final states at all
The variable is not always a natural number, for example it goes negative or takes values like 1/2, 1/4, ...
questions.explanation: If it were always a natural number, it could fall at most x(q0) times. Endless decrease is only possible with negative or non-integer values.
